scope_note: Family-recognition backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Restores Acer to the family map, reconciles old western-soapberry names, and builds a local three-genus visual framework around Acer, Sapindus, and Ungnadia.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start with fruit and leaf arrangement, not a single leaf shape. In the local learner, Acer has opposite leaves and paired samaras; Sapindus has alternate pinnate leaves and amber/orange drupe-like soapberries; Ungnadia has alternate pinnate leaves and a 3-lobed, 3-valved woody capsule.
family_lesson.strongest_family_confirmation: Woody plant with stipules usually absent; flowers often small/functionally unisexual with a conspicuous floral disk; superior 2–3-carpellate ovary; fruit often conspicuously lobed or winged and may become a samara, drupe, or capsule.
core_characters: Trees or shrubs in the local learner.
Leaves may be alternate or opposite and simple or compound; Sapindaceae cannot be learned from one leaf arrangement.
Flowers commonly 4–5-merous, often functionally unisexual, with a floral/nectar disk.
Stamens commonly 8, though the family is variable.
Fruit exceptionally diverse: samaras/schizocarps, drupes, or capsules all occur in the local learner.
Modern Sapindaceae includes Acer (maples), which older sources may place in Aceraceae.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach Sapindaceae as always alternate-leaved: Acer is opposite-leaved.
Do not teach Sapindaceae as always compound-leaved: many Acer species have simple palmately lobed leaves.
Do not teach one fruit type as the family character; local fruit spans paired samaras, drupes, and capsules.
Do not treat every western-soapberry source using Sapindus saponaria var. drummondii as a separate taxon; current POWO accepts Sapindus drummondii.
Do not count cultivated Acer palmatum toward native metrics.

fastest_cues: Fruit a paired schizocarp splitting into two winged samaras.
Acer negundo is unusual among maples in having odd-pinnate compound leaves.
Acer.field_teaching: Opposite compound leaves can suggest ash, but paired maple samaras immediately separate boxelder from Fraxinus.

fastest_cues: Fruit becomes a translucent amber/orange-brown 1–2(–3)-lobed drupe/mericarp with a hard dark seed.
Aborted carpels can remain visible at the base of the developed fruit.
Sapindus.field_teaching: The soapberry fruit is the fastest visual anchor; pair it with the pinnate leaf and panicle.

fastest_cues: Showy rosy-pink flowers appear before or with new leaves on older wood.
Fruit is a distinctive pear-shaped 3-lobed/3-valved woody capsule.
Capsule opens to expose glossy dark buckeye-like seeds.
Ungnadia.field_teaching: Mexican buckeye looks nothing like a maple fruit or soapberry fruit; the woody 3-valved capsule is the genus-level giveaway.

fast_key: Opposite leaves + paired winged samaras -> Acer.
Opposite odd-pinnate leaf with 3–5 leaflets + paired samaras -> Acer negundo.
Alternate pinnate leaves + translucent orange/amber drupe-like fruits -> Sapindus drummondii framework.
Alternate pinnate leaves + pink flowers + woody 3-valved pear-shaped capsule -> Ungnadia speciosa.
Compound leaves plus resinous sap drying black -> reconsider Anacardiaceae.
Compound aromatic leaves with pellucid oil dots -> reconsider Rutaceae.

sapindus_saponaria_sensu_stricto.reason: POWO treats S. saponaria as a separate accepted tropical/subtropical species and does not list Texas among its native areas. The project Hays-local flag may reflect older Texas use of a broad S. saponaria concept that included western soapberry.

Anacardiaceae.confusion: Both can be woody with alternate compound leaves and small flowers; some fruits are drupe-like.
Anacardiaceae.tie_breaker: Kew notes Sapindaceae trees/shrubs generally lack resinous sap, whereas Anacardiaceae often has resin that dries brown/black. Sapindaceae also commonly has lobed/winged fruit and a floral disk.

Rutaceae.confusion: Compound leaves and small flowers can overlap.
Rutaceae.tie_breaker: Rutaceae has regular pellucid oil-gland dots and strong citrus/rank odor; Sapindaceae lacks those regular translucent gland dots.

Fraxinus_Oleaceae.confusion: Acer negundo has opposite compound leaves and can look ash-like.
Fraxinus_Oleaceae.tie_breaker: Acer produces paired samaras; Fraxinus produces single samaras. Boxelder also has maple-type paired fruit clusters rather than ash keys.

Juglandaceae.confusion: Sapindus and Ungnadia can look generally walnut-like in leaf silhouette.
Juglandaceae.tie_breaker: Juglandaceae reproductive structures are catkins plus a husked nut; local Sapindaceae uses panicles/showy flowers and samara/drupe/capsule fruits.
